newsitem.title: BULGARIA: CURRENCY BOARD LAST CHANCE FOR BULGARIA - PRESIDENT.
newsitem.headline: CURRENCY BOARD LAST CHANCE FOR BULGARIA - PRESIDENT.

text.p: President Zhelyu Zhelev said on Thursday a strict IMF-proposed monetary regime was Bulgaria's last chance to rescue the economy and politicians must work together to implement it.
Prime Minister Zhan Videnov said on Monday the government and central bank had accepted an International Monetary Fund (IMF) proposal for a currency board system to be put in place early next year.
"This is the last chance for our country to save democracy and secure its progress," Zhelev said in a speech broadcast on state radio and television.
"If we miss that chance, it will be the worst possible sentence for the country's whole political model and worst of all, the impact of this failure will pursue us into the next century."

Videnov's acceptance of the currency board infuriated Zhelev's opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), as the IMF had said a broad political consensus should be reached before a decision was made.
The measure must be debated and voted by parliament, in which the Socialists have a secure majority.
Zhelev wrote to IMF director-general Michel Camdessus on Thursday warning that while quick action on the economy was vital, the proposal lacked broad-based support.
"I received an answer from Mr Camdessus saying he was very concerned that the waste of financial assets and people's money in Bulgaria had been going on too long already," Zhelev said.

"In the letter he also noted that there is a lack of confidence in the ability of the Bulgarian government to stabilise the economy and to support market-oriented institutions which are vital for economic development."

Under the currency board mechanism, which aims to restore confidence and defeat hyperinflation, central bank lending to commercial banks and the government is cut, and money in circulation must be strictly matched with central bank hard currency reserves.
The lev has depreciated steadily this year and suffered further sharp falls last week as panicked Bulgarians rushed to convert their savings to dollars.

The UDF has said it will not support a currency board if it is implemented by the Socialist government and it wants early elections, but Videnov's decision to set up the board as soon as possible weakens its position.
At the same time, it strengthens Videnov against his critics in the divided Socialist party ahead of next month's party congress called to discuss calls for policy changes and a cabinet shuffle.

Videnov's most prominent critic, Foreign Minister Georgi Pirinski, resigned last month saying the government was unable to handle the crisis and he would devote himself to preparing for the congress, but Videnov has not yet presented the resignation to parliament for approval, leaving Pirinski in limbo.
